name: Gangtok
tagline: Sikkim's ridge-top capital and base for the north and east
meta_description: Gangtok guide: MG Marg, Enchey and Rumtek monasteries, Namgyal Institute of Tibetology, permits for Tsomgo and North Sikkim, stays, costs and getting there.
summary: Gangtok is Sikkim's capital, spread along a ridge at about 1,650 m above the Ranikhola valley. It has been the seat of government since 1894. Use it as the base for Tsomgo Lake, Nathu La and North Sikkim permits, and give it two days of its own for MG Marg, its monasteries and the Tibetology institute.
intro: Gangtok climbs a ridge in tiers of concrete and prayer flags, with the Ranikhola river far below to the west and, on clear mornings, Kangchenjunga to the north-west. The town grew after 1894, when the Chogyal Thutob Namgyal moved the royal capital here from Tumlong, and it became the state capital when Sikkim joined India in 1975. Today it is a compact, orderly city where most life happens along a few long roads linked by steep stairways.

The centre is MG Marg, a pedestrian street of shops, cafes and benches where smoking and littering are banned. Below it lies Lal Bazaar, the old market, and above it the palace complex and the Tsuklakhang royal chapel. Enchey monastery sits on the ridge to the north-east, the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology and the Do Drul Chorten to the south, and Rumtek, the largest monastery in Sikkim, across the valley about 24 km away.

Gangtok is also where you sort out the rest of Sikkim. Registered travel agencies arrange the Protected Area Permits for Tsomgo, Nathu La, North Sikkim and Zuluk, usually a day in advance. Shared jeeps leave from the Vajra and Deorali stands for Siliguri, Namchi, Gyalshing and Mangan. Plan at least two nights here at the start and one at the end.

highlights.title: MG Marg in the evening
highlights.text: Gangtok's main street is closed to traffic and kept spotless, with benches down the middle and the town's cafes, bakeries and bookshops on either side. Walk it after 6 pm, when families come out, then drop down the stairs to Lal Bazaar for local produce and chhurpi.

highlights.title: Enchey monastery on the ridge
highlights.text: A small Nyingma monastery built in 1909 on the ridge about 3 km above the centre, among tall pines. The prayer hall is painted inside with guardian deities, and monks perform cham masked dances here in the winter months before Losar.

highlights.title: Namgyal Institute of Tibetology
highlights.text: A research institute and museum in a traditional Sikkimese building, opened in 1958, holding thangkas, statues, ritual objects and one of the largest collections of Tibetan texts outside Tibet. Next door, the Do Drul Chorten is ringed by 108 prayer wheels.

highlights.title: Rumtek monastery
highlights.text: About 24 km from town across the Ranipool valley, Rumtek was built in the 1960s as the seat of the Karma Kagyu school in exile. The main hall, the golden stupa and the monastic college sit on a quiet hillside; carry photo ID for the security check.

highlights.title: Viewpoints for Kangchenjunga
highlights.text: On a clear morning, Ganesh Tok, Tashi viewpoint and Hanuman Tok all look across to Kangchenjunga and its neighbours. Go before 7 am in October to December; cloud usually builds by mid-morning.

highlights.title: The ropeway
highlights.text: A cable car runs between Deorali, near the Tibetology institute, and Tashiling near the secretariat, giving a slow view over the town and valley for a small fare. Queues are long at weekends in season.

field_notes.fact: Gangtok became Sikkim's capital in 1894, when the ruler Thutob Namgyal shifted the royal seat from Tumlong in the north. Before that it was a small hermitage and village.
Enchey monastery was built in 1909 on a site associated with Lama Druptob Karpo, a tantric master said in local tradition to have flown to this hill from Maenam.
The foundation stone of the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology was laid by the 14th Dalai Lama in 1957, and the institute was opened by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru in 1958.

how_to_reach.text: Bagdogra Airport near Siliguri is the main gateway, about 125 km and 4–5 hours by road. Sikkim Tourism runs a counter there, and foreigners can get their Restricted Area Permit on arrival. Pakyong Airport, about 30 km from Gangtok, has had only limited flights; check current status before you travel.

New Jalpaiguri (NJP) is the nearest major railway station, with trains from Kolkata, Delhi and Guwahati. Shared jeeps and taxis wait outside, and Siliguri's SNT bus stand is about 5 km away. A railway line to Rangpo is under construction.

The NH10 runs from Siliguri up the Teesta valley to Rangpo and Singtam, then climbs to Gangtok, about 115 km. Shared jeeps run all day; SNT buses leave in the morning. Landslides close sections in the monsoon and traffic may be diverted through Kalimpong; check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Saver: guesthouses and small hotels around Tibet Road, Arithang and Lal Bazaar offer doubles from about ₹1,500–2,500, and many have their own permit desks. Comfort: Hotel Tibet near Paljor Stadium and Netuk House, a family-run heritage home off Tibet Road, are reliable picks in the centre. Signature: the Elgin Nor-Khill, a 1930s royal guest house below the stadium, and the Mayfair Spa Resort and Casino outside the centre are the city's best-known high-end stays.
tips: Apply for North Sikkim and Tsomgo permits through your hotel or a registered agency the day you arrive; carry ID and passport photos.
Walk rather than drive in the centre; one-way roads make short taxi rides slow and expensive.
Plastic bags are banned, and littering and smoking on MG Marg are fined; carry a cloth bag.
Remove shoes and walk clockwise inside monasteries, and ask before photographing monks or prayer halls.
Keep the last night of your trip in Gangtok so a landslide on the way back from the north does not cost you a flight.

experiences.title: An evening on MG Marg and in Lal Bazaar
experiences.cost: Free to walk; food ₹300–700 per person
experiences.summary: Walk Gangtok's car-free main street at dusk, then take the stairways down to Lal Bazaar for chhurpi, fermented greens and street momos. It is the easiest way to see how the city eats, shops and spends its evenings.
body: MG Marg runs for about a kilometre along the ridge, paved, lined with benches and planters and closed to vehicles. The rules are strict: no smoking, no spitting, no littering, and local police enforce them. In the evening, families, students and office workers stroll its length, and the cafes and bakeries fill. It feels more like a town square than a street.

From the lower end, steps lead down to Lal Bazaar, now housed in the multi-level Kanchenjunga shopping complex. Here farmers from the surrounding hills sell chhurpi, both soft and hard, dried gundruk, fiddlehead ferns in season, local cherry peppers called dalle khursani and heaps of greens. It is one of the best places to see what Sikkim's organic farms actually grow.

For food, look for small canteens serving thukpa, thenthuk, momos and sha phaley, a fried bread stuffed with meat or cabbage. Prices are low and portions generous. Fermented foods are part of everyday cooking in Sikkim; try a little gundruk soup or kinema, fermented soybean, if you see it. Dalle chillies are very hot; taste carefully.

faqs.q: Is MG Marg free to visit?
faqs.a: Yes. MG Marg is a public pedestrian street with no entry fee. Shops and cafes open from morning to about 8 or 9 pm. Smoking, spitting and littering carry fines, so use the bins provided.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Gangtok?
faqs.a: Try thukpa, momos, thenthuk, sha phaley and gundruk soup at local canteens, and pick up chhurpi in Lal Bazaar. Most plates cost ₹80–180. Ask for dalle chilli on the side; it is very hot.

faqs.q: Is Lal Bazaar open every day?
faqs.a: Lal Bazaar is open most days, with the busiest trading at the weekend when farmers bring produce from nearby villages. Some stalls close on certain weekdays, so go on Saturday or Sunday morning for the fullest market.

experiences.title: Rumtek monastery and the golden stupa
experiences.cost: Entry free or a small fee; taxi ₹1,500–2,500 return
experiences.summary: Cross the valley to Rumtek, the largest monastery in Sikkim, rebuilt in the 1960s as the seat of the Karma Kagyu lineage outside Tibet. See the main assembly hall, the golden reliquary stupa and the monastic college, and hear the afternoon chanting.
body: Rumtek sits on a hillside about 24 km from Gangtok, a drive of roughly an hour via Ranipool. An older Kagyu monastery stood here from the 18th century; the present complex was built in the 1960s by the 16th Karmapa after he left Tibet, and it follows the design of the lineage's original seat at Tsurphu. Arriving through the gate, you climb past monks' quarters to a wide courtyard facing the main hall.

The assembly hall is richly painted, with large statues and thousands of small images of the Buddha. Behind it, a separate hall houses a golden stupa containing relics of the 16th Karmapa. Above the main complex is the monastic college, the Karma Shri Nalanda Institute, where young monks study philosophy. Mid-morning and mid-afternoon you may hear the chanting of prayers.

There is a security check at the gate, so carry a photo ID. Photography is not allowed inside the halls. Dress modestly, walk clockwise and keep your voice low. The old Rumtek monastery, a short walk below, is smaller and quieter. Combine the visit with Lingdum monastery on the way back if you have time.

faqs.q: How far is Rumtek from Gangtok?
faqs.a: About 24 km, an hour by road via Ranipool. A taxi for a half-day return trip costs roughly ₹1,500–2,500. Shared jeeps run from Gangtok towards Rumtek but are less frequent.

faqs.q: Can I take photos at Rumtek?
faqs.a: You can photograph the courtyard and exterior, but photography inside the halls is not permitted. Ask before photographing monks, and avoid flash anywhere near shrines.

faqs.q: Do I need ID to visit Rumtek monastery?
faqs.a: Yes, carry a photo ID such as an Aadhaar card or passport. There is a security check at the entrance, and foreigners may be asked for their permit details.

experiences.title: Tibetology museum and the Do Drul Chorten
experiences.best_time: 10 am–4 pm; closed on some holidays
experiences.summary: Spend a morning with Sikkim's best collection of Buddhist art at the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology, then walk five minutes uphill to the Do Drul Chorten, a white stupa ringed by 108 prayer wheels. Together they explain much of what you will see in monasteries across the state.
body: The Namgyal Institute of Tibetology stands in a garden in Deorali, south of the centre. The building follows traditional Sikkimese style, with painted windows and a sloping roof. Opened in 1958, it was founded to support research on the language and culture of Tibet and the Buddhist Himalaya, and it holds a large library of manuscripts and block prints.

The museum on the ground floor is small but rich: thangka scroll paintings, bronze statues, ritual masks, old coins and objects from Sikkim's monasteries, with labels in English. It is a good primer before Pemayangtse, Rumtek or the cham dances. Check opening days before you go, as it closes on Sundays and some public holidays.

A short walk up the road, the Do Drul Chorten was built in 1945 and is surrounded by 108 prayer wheels, turned clockwise by pilgrims walking around it. A smaller shrine nearby holds large statues of Guru Rinpoche. The cable car station is also at Deorali, so you can combine the visit with a ride across town.

faqs.q: What are the opening hours of the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology?
faqs.a: It has generally opened on weekdays and Saturday from about 10 am to 4 pm, closing on Sunday and some holidays. Hours can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Tibetology museum worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, especially early in your trip. Its thangkas, statues and ritual objects explain the art and symbols you will see in Sikkim's monasteries, and it takes only an hour or two.

faqs.q: How do I walk around the Do Drul Chorten?
faqs.a: Walk clockwise around the stupa, keeping it on your right, and turn the prayer wheels with your right hand as you pass. Remove hats inside the shrine and keep your voice low.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Gangtok?
faqs.a: Two full days cover MG Marg, Enchey, the Tibetology institute, Rumtek and a viewpoint, plus a third day for the Tsomgo Lake permit trip. If you are going to North Sikkim, add a night at either end, since tours start and finish in Gangtok.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Gangtok?
faqs.a: March to May and October to December. Spring brings flowers and pleasant days around 15–22 °C; autumn gives the clearest mountain views. June to September is monsoon, with landslides on the NH10. Winter is cold but dry and good value.

faqs.q: How do I go from Bagdogra Airport to Gangtok?
faqs.a: Take a pre-paid or app-booked taxi for about ₹3,500–5,000, 4–5 hours, or go to Siliguri and take a shared jeep or SNT bus for a few hundred rupees. Foreign nationals can get their Sikkim permit at the airport counter.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Gangtok?
faqs.a: Indian nationals do not need a permit for Gangtok. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, available free at Bagdogra Airport, the Rangpo and Melli check posts, Sikkim Tourism offices and online. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get permits for Tsomgo and North Sikkim from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Registered travel agencies and most hotels apply for the Protected Area Permits for you. Give them a copy of photo ID and two passport photos, ideally a day ahead. Permits are issued for specific dates and vehicles, so you travel with that agency.

faqs.q: Is Gangtok good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes. The town is clean and calm, MG Marg is traffic-free, and there are easy outings such as the ropeway, monasteries and viewpoints. Take care on the Tsomgo and Nathu La trip with young children because of altitude; talk to your doctor first.

faqs.q: Where should I stay in Gangtok?
faqs.a: Stay within walking distance of MG Marg, on Tibet Road, Paljor Stadium Road or around Arithang, so you can walk in the evening. Budget rooms start around ₹1,500 a night; good mid-range hotels cost ₹4,000–8,000; the top hotels charge more.

Gangtok is generally safe, and MG Marg is busy and well lit until about 9 pm. Most shops close early, and the town is quiet after 10 pm. Use registered taxis, and take care on steep stairways after dark.
Yes, Gangtok has many ATMs and card payments are common in hotels and larger shops. Withdraw enough cash before heading to North Sikkim, Zuluk or Yuksom, where ATMs are few and homestays expect cash.
